Buying Guides

Choose the right gear — and the right spec to resell

Short, practical guides from the sourcing side of the table. The same checks we run at the factory are the ones that matter in the field — and the ones your customers will judge you by.

How to Choose a Camping Tent

Capacity ratings assume slim sleepers side by side — for comfort, size up one person. Then check these three specs before price:

  • Waterproof rating: 2000mm is fine for summer rain; 3000mm+ for real storms
  • Poles: fiberglass is budget-friendly; aluminum is lighter and lasts longer
  • Two doors & vestibules matter more than floor space for 3–4 person tents

Reselling? The 2-person dome is the volume staple in most markets — its OEM price is quoted by quantity tier, starting from the reference range on the product card.

Backpack Capacity: 40L, 60L or 80L?

Match volume to trip length, not ambition — an oversized pack just gets filled with weight.

  • 30–40L: day hikes and overnight trips with compact gear
  • 50–65L: the sweet spot for 3–5 day trips — our 60L covers most buyers
  • 70L+: winter trips or expeditions carrying bulky insulation

Also check the back system: an adjustable torso and padded hip belt sell better than extra pockets.

First Wholesale Order? Read This First

How experienced importers keep a first factory order low-risk:

  • Start with samples — one piece of each line, checked against the spec sheet
  • Mix categories in one shipment to spread freight cost across more SKUs
  • Confirm MOQ, lead time and packing data in writing before paying a deposit
  • Ask for pre-shipment photos/video of your actual batch — we send them as standard

Request the free catalog and we'll suggest a starter mix for your market.

Sleeping Bag Temperature Ratings, Explained

Under the ISO/EN test standard, every rated bag carries three numbers — and they are not interchangeable:

  • Comfort rating: the lowest temperature at which an average sleeper stays warm all night — this is the number that matters
  • Limit rating: the point where a warm sleeper can just manage, curled up, without waking from cold
  • Extreme rating: a survival figure only — the sleeper stays alive, but cold and uncomfortable

Always sell on the comfort rating, never the extreme number. A customer who buys a bag by its extreme rating will be cold on the first real night out — and will return it.

Fill and shape decide the rest. Down packs smaller and lighter for its warmth, but costs more and loses insulation when wet. Synthetic fill is bulkier and heavier, yet keeps working when damp and suits budget lines. Mummy shapes trap heat efficiently for cold nights; rectangular bags feel roomier and sell well for car camping and mild weather.

Reselling? A 3-season bag is the volume staple for spring-to-autumn camping — it covers the nights most customers actually camp. Our 3-Season Sleeping Bag is built for exactly that slot in your range.

Quick checklist:

  • Quote and compare the comfort rating, not the extreme
  • Match fill to your market: down for weight-conscious hikers, synthetic for value and wet climates
  • Mummy for cold-weather lines, rectangular for comfort camping
  • Check packed size and weight against your freight costs

How to Choose a Rechargeable Headlamp

Lumens measure total light output, not how far the beam actually reaches. A focused beam throws usable light much further than a wide flood at the same lumen count — so check the stated beam distance, and think about whether your customers need spot, flood, or both.

  • Rechargeable beats disposable: no battery purchases, no spares to carry, and a far easier resale story — USB-C charging is now the expected standard
  • Runtime: judge a lamp by its hours on medium mode, not the headline figure on turbo
  • Water resistance: IPX4 shrugs off rain splashes; IPX6 and above handle heavy downpours
  • Red-light mode preserves night vision and doesn't disturb tentmates; a tilting head aims the beam at a map, a stove, or the trail without neck strain

Reselling? Headlamps are a classic low-MOQ add-on item for camping orders — small, light, cheap to ship, and easy to bundle with tents and bags. Our Rechargeable LED Headlamp is stocked for exactly that role.

Quick checklist:

  • Compare beam distance, not just lumens
  • USB-C rechargeable, with runtime quoted on a usable mode
  • IPX4 minimum for rain; higher if your market camps wet
  • Red-light mode and an adjustable tilt head

How to Choose Trekking Poles

Poles take load off knees on descents, add stability on rough ground, and set a rhythm on climbs. The right pair depends on material, locking system, and the terrain your customers actually walk.

  • Material: aluminium is tougher against knocks and cheaper to replace; carbon is noticeably lighter and absorbs vibration better, but costs more and can crack under a hard side impact
  • Length adjustment & locking: look for a clear height scale and a lever-style quick lock that clamps tight without tools — twist locks are compact but can slip when grit gets in
  • Grip: cork grips mould to the hand and stay comfortable on long days; foam is lighter and budget-friendly; rubber suits cold-weather use
  • Basket & tip: small baskets for summer trails, wide snow baskets for winter; a carbide tip grips rock and ice, with rubber feet for paved paths

Reselling? Poles are a natural add-on to backpack and tent orders — light, compact to ship, and easy to bundle. Our Folding Trekking Poles fold down small for packing, which makes them a practical line for hikers who travel to the trailhead.

Quick checklist:

  • Aluminium for durability and value, carbon for minimum weight
  • Lever quick-locks that hold firm and adjust without tools
  • Grip material matched to your market's climate and trip length
  • Basket size matched to season and terrain

How to Choose a Folding Camping Chair

A camp chair is judged in the first ten seconds a customer sits down — and again at pack-up time. Four specs decide whether it earns repeat orders or returns.

  • Weight capacity: check the rated load, not just how sturdy the frame looks — and leave a margin above your typical user's weight
  • Folded size & carry weight: a chair that folds flat or packs into a carry bag sells to car campers and festival-goers alike; the lighter it carries, the wider the market
  • Frame & fabric: steel frames are strong and economical, aluminium frames cut weight; look for a tough, easy-clean fabric such as Oxford weave with reinforced stitching at stress points
  • Comfort extras: a footrest turns a chair into a lounger for long evenings, and a cup holder plus a side pocket keep drinks and phones off the ground

Reselling? Chairs are a volume line for car-camping and glamping ranges, and they pair well with family tents in the same shipment. Our Folding Camping Chair with Footrest covers the comfort end of that range — the footrest and cup holder are exactly the features customers mention in reviews.

Quick checklist:

  • Rated capacity with a comfortable safety margin
  • Folded size and carry weight that suit your customers' transport
  • Frame material and fabric matched to price point and use
  • Footrest, cup holder and storage pocket for the comfort segment

How to Choose a Portable Camping Stove

A camp stove is judged on how reliably it boils water and cooks a simple meal outdoors — in wind, on uneven ground, and when pack space is tight. Five points separate a stove customers keep from one they leave behind:

  • Fuel type: a screw-on gas canister is the simplest system for most campers — the stove threads directly onto the canister, with no priming, pumping or liquid fuel to handle, and canisters are widely available for backpacking and car camping alike
  • Heat output & boil time: in general terms, higher heat output brings water to a boil faster, but uses fuel more quickly; a stove that also simmers well gives more cooking control and stretches a canister further — judge boil time alongside fuel efficiency, not on speed alone
  • Piezo ignition: a built-in push-button piezo igniter lights the burner without matches or a separate lighter — a convenience most buyers now expect, though a backup lighter is still worth packing
  • Weight & packed size: for hikers, look for a compact design with folding pot supports that packs down small and carries light; for car camping, a little extra bulk matters far less than stability
  • Pot stability & wind resistance: wide, sturdy pot supports and a low, stable stance keep pans from tipping, while a burner design that shelters the flame helps it stay lit and boil efficiently in a breeze

Reselling? Stoves are a natural companion line to tents and cookware in the same shipment — compact to stock and easy to explain. Our Portable Camping Stove is a portable canister-top option suited to that role in a camping kitchen range.

Quick checklist:

  • Screw-on gas canister fitting for simple, widely available fuel
  • Heat output balanced for reasonably fast boiling and good simmer control
  • Built-in piezo ignition, with a backup lighter in the kit
  • Weight and packed size matched to hiking or car-camping use
  • Stable pot supports and a flame that holds up in wind

How to Choose a Camping Lantern

A lantern lights a whole tent or camp table rather than a single spot, so even, glare-free light matters more than a headline brightness figure. Five points decide whether a lantern earns its place in the kit:

  • Brightness & light modes: in general terms, look for more than one brightness level so the light can be turned down for inside a tent and up for cooking or group use; a choice of warm and white light is a plus — warm light feels softer for evenings in camp, while white light is clearer for tasks — and a dim or night mode helps the battery last and avoids waking tentmates
  • Battery type & runtime: a built-in rechargeable battery avoids a steady supply of disposables; judge runtime on a medium setting rather than the lowest glow, and consider how many nights of typical use one charge needs to cover between top-ups
  • USB charging & power-bank function: USB charging lets the lantern refill from a car, a laptop or a solar panel while travelling, and a lantern that can also work as a power bank gives campers a handy backup source for topping up a phone or headlamp in camp
  • Weight & hanging options: for hikers, lighter carries better and every gram counts; for car camping, a little extra size matters less. A top handle or hanging hook lets the lantern hang from a tent loop or branch so the light spreads from above, while a flat, stable base keeps it steady on a table
  • Water resistance: camp light lives outdoors, so look for a lantern described as splash-resistant at minimum for use in rain and around wet ground; models built to handle heavier rain suit exposed or wet-climate camping — check the stated rating before assuming it can be left out in a downpour

Reselling? Lanterns are an easy add-on to tent and camp-furniture orders — one light serves a whole pitch, so most campers buy them without much persuasion. Our USB Camping Lantern & Power Bank is a rechargeable option in that role, combining tent and table light with a backup charging function for small devices in camp.

Quick checklist:

  • Several brightness levels, with warm and white light if your market values evening comfort
  • Rechargeable battery, with runtime judged on a usable medium setting
  • USB charging, and a power-bank function for topping up small devices
  • Weight matched to hiking or car-camping use, plus a handle or hook for hanging
  • Water resistance suited to rain and wet campsites

How to Choose a Packable Windbreaker

A packable windbreaker is the layer hikers and travellers reach for when the weather is changeable — wind, a chill, or a passing shower rather than a full storm. Six points decide whether one earns its space in the pack:

  • Waterproof vs water-resistant: the two terms are not the same. A water-resistant finish sheds light drizzle, mist and brief showers and dries quickly, but will soak through in sustained rain. A fully waterproof jacket uses a membrane or coating with sealed seams to keep prolonged rain out — it offers more protection, but is usually less breathable, bulkier and more expensive. Most windbreakers sit on the water-resistant side of that line, and that is the right trade-off for their job
  • Breathability: a windbreaker blocks the chill of the wind while still letting heat and moisture vapour escape during effort. That balance is what makes it comfortable for walking, cycling and travel — a layer that traps sweat will feel clammy on the first climb, so look for a fabric described as breathable, and ventilation details where they are offered
  • Packability & packed size: the defining feature of the category — the jacket should pack away small, ideally into its own pocket or an attached stuff pouch, so it can live in a daypack, hand luggage or glove box and be pulled out only when the weather turns
  • Weight: a packable windbreaker should feel light to carry and easy to forget about until it is needed. Lighter styles suit hikers and travellers who count every item; a slightly more substantial fabric can feel more durable for everyday wear — match the weight to how and where it will be used
  • Hood & zip details: a hood that adjusts or packs away keeps wind and light rain off the head and neck without flapping; a smooth, full-length front zip makes the layer easy to put on, take off and vent. Details worth checking are elasticated or adjustable cuffs and hem to seal out draughts, secure zipped pockets for a phone and keys, and a chin guard or storm flap where fitted

When is a windbreaker enough, and when do you need a rain jacket? A windbreaker is enough for breezy ridges, cool evenings, light drizzle and changeable days, and as a general travel and commuting layer where breathability and low packed size matter most. Step up to a dedicated waterproof rain jacket for prolonged or heavy rain, cold and wet conditions, or trips where staying dry for hours at a time is essential — in those conditions a water-resistant layer will eventually let water through.

Reselling? A packable windbreaker is an easy line to range alongside backpacks and travel gear — it suits a wide range of customers, from hikers to everyday commuters, and needs little explanation. Our Packable Windbreaker Jacket is a lightweight, packable option in that role, made to be carried just in case and worn as a handy wind- and light-shower layer for the trail, travel and daily use.

Quick checklist:

  • Water-resistant for wind and light showers; fully waterproof only if sustained rain is expected
  • Breathable fabric that blocks wind without trapping sweat
  • Packs away small — ideally into its own pocket or pouch
  • Light enough to carry as a just-in-case layer
  • Adjustable or pack-away hood, smooth full-length zip, and secure zipped pockets

How to Choose an Insulated Stainless Steel Bottle

A good insulated bottle keeps drinks at a pleasant temperature through a working day, a hike, or a long drive — without leaking in a bag or picking up flavours from yesterday's drink. Five points decide whether one earns repeat orders:

  • Double-wall vacuum insulation: two walls of stainless steel with the air drawn out of the space between them. With almost no air to carry heat across, warmth and cold move very slowly between the inside and the outside — so a hot drink stays hot and a cold drink stays cold far longer than in a single-wall bottle, and the outer wall stays comfortable to hold
  • Capacity choice: match the size to the use rather than buying the biggest bottle on the shelf. A smaller bottle suits a desk, a school bag or a short walk and is easier to carry; a mid-size bottle is the all-rounder for a full day out; a larger bottle suits long trips, group use or anyone who cannot refill often — but remember a bigger bottle is heavier to carry once filled
  • Lid types: a screw-on lid seals simply and reliably and is the safest choice for carrying inside a bag; a flip-top or straw lid allows one-handed drinking while walking, cycling or driving; a wide-mouth lid is easiest to fill, to add ice to, and to clean. Whichever style you choose, check that the seal sits firmly and the lid closes with a positive, leak-resistant fit
  • Weight & packability: stainless steel carries more weight than plastic, and insulation adds a little more, so judge the bottle by how it will actually be carried. For hikers and commuters, a slimmer shape that fits a pack's side pocket or a car cup holder matters as much as the weight itself; for car camping and home use, a sturdier, wider bottle is easier to live with
  • Cleaning & durability: stainless steel resists dents and knocks, does not hold on to flavours or odours the way plastic can, and wipes clean inside and out. A wide mouth makes washing simpler and helps the bottle dry properly between uses; a smooth, well-finished rim and a simple lid design with few hidden corners are easier to keep hygienic over years of daily use

Reselling? Insulated bottles are an easy, year-round line to range alongside backpacks and travel gear — they suit commuters, students, drivers and hikers alike, and need very little explanation at the shelf. Our Stainless Steel Bottle 750ml is a sturdy stainless option in that role, made for everyday carrying, day trips and camp use.

Quick checklist:

  • Double-wall vacuum insulation for drinks that stay hot or cold longer
  • Capacity matched to the use — smaller for daily carrying, larger for long days without refills
  • Lid style matched to the buyer: screw-on for leak-safe carrying, flip or straw for one-handed drinking, wide mouth for easy filling and cleaning
  • Weight and shape that suit the pack, bag or cup holder it will travel in
  • Durable stainless steel that cleans easily and does not retain flavours
